key_findings.claim: The proposed Inception-v3 architecture achieves new state-of-the-art performance for single-crop evaluation on the ILSVRC 2012 classification challenge.
key_findings.evidence: 21.2% top-1 and 5.6% top-5 error for single frame evaluation using a network with a computational cost of 5 billion multiply-adds per inference and with using less than 25 million parameters (Abstract). Our highest quality version of Inception-v3 reaches 21.2%, top-1 and 5.6% top-5 error for single crop evaluation on the ILSVR 2012 classification, setting a new state of the art (Conclusion).

key_findings.claim: An ensemble of Inception-v3 models achieves new state-of-the-art performance with multi-crop evaluation on the ILSVRC 2012 classification benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: With an ensemble of 4 models and multi-crop evaluation, we report 3.5% top-5 error and 17.3% top-1 error (Abstract). Our ensemble of four Inception-v3 models reaches 3.5% with multi-crop evaluation reaches 3.5% top-5 error which represents an over 25% reduction to the best published results and is almost half of the error of ILSVRC 2014 winining GoogLeNet ensemble (Conclusion).
key_findings.limitations: All results, but the top-5 ensemble result reported are on the validation set. The ensemble yielded 3.46% top-5 error on the validation set (Table 5 footnote). In the upcoming version of this paper, we will verify our ensemble result on the test set (Results).

key_findings.claim: High quality recognition performance can be achieved with lower receptive field resolutions (e.g., 79x79) if computational effort is kept constant.
key_findings.evidence: Although the lower-resolution networks take longer to train, the quality of the final result is quite close to that of their higher resolution counterparts (Methodology, referring to Table 2). We have also demonstrated that high quality results can be reached with receptive field resolution as low as 79×79 (Conclusion).
key_findings.limitations: If one would just naively reduce the network size according to the input resolution, then network would perform much more poorly. However this would an unfair comparison as we would are comparing a 16 times cheaper model on a more difficult task (Methodology).

key_findings.claim: Several general design principles are proposed for efficiently scaling up convolutional networks.
key_findings.evidence: In this paper, we start with describing a few general principles and optimization ideas that that proved to be useful for scaling up convolution networks in efficient ways (Introduction). Here we will describe a few design principles based on large-scale experimentation with various architectural choices with convolutional networks (Proposed Solution).
key_findings.limitations: At this point, the utility of the principles below are speculative and additional future experimental evidence will be necessary to assess their accuracy and domain of validity. Still, grave deviations from these principles tended to result in deterioration in the quality of the networks and fixing situations where those deviations were detected resulted in improved architectures in general. Although these principles might make sense, it is not straightforward to use them to improve the quality of networks out of box. The idea is to use them judiciously in ambiguous situations only (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: Replacing 5x5 convolutions with two layers of 3x3 convolutions reduces computational cost and parameter count.
key_findings.evidence: Sliding this small network over the input activation grid boils down to replacing the 5 × 5 convolution with two layers of 3 × 3 convolution (compare Figure 4 with 5). This way, we end up with a net 9+9 / 25 × reduction of computation, resulting in a relative gain of 28% by this factorization. The exact same saving holds for the parameter count as each parameter is used exactly once in the computation of the activation of each unit (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: Using rectified linear units (ReLUs) is superior to linear activations in all stages of convolution factorization.
key_findings.evidence: We have ran several control experiments (for example see figure 2) and using linear activation was always inferior to using rectified linear units in all stages of the factorization. We attribute this gain to the enhanced space of variations that the network can learn especially if we batch-normalize [7] the output activations (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: Asymmetric convolutions (e.g., n x 1 followed by 1 x n) can factorize larger convolutions (e.g., 3x3) more efficiently than symmetric smaller convolutions (e.g., 2x2).
key_findings.evidence: Using a 3 × 1 convolution followed by a 1 × 3 convolution is equivalent to sliding a two layer network with the same receptive field as in a 3 × 3 convolution. Still the two-layer solution is 33% cheaper for the same number of output filters, if the number of input and output filters is equal. By comparison, factorizing a 3 × 3 convolution into a two 2 × 2 convolution represents only a 11% saving of computation (Proposed Solution).
key_findings.limitations: Employing this factorization does not work well on early layers, but it gives very good results on medium grid-sizes (On m×m feature maps, where m ranges between 12 and 20) (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: Auxiliary classifiers primarily act as regularizers, rather than aiding early convergence or evolving low-level features.
key_findings.evidence: Interestingly, we found that auxiliary classifiers did not result in improved convergence early in the training: the training progression of network with and without side head looks virtually identical before both models reach high accuracy. Near the end of training, the network with the auxiliary branches starts to overtake the accuracy of the network without any auxiliary branch and reaches a slightly higher plateau. Instead, we argue that the auxiliary classifiers act as regularizer. This is supported by the fact that the main classifier of the network performs better if the side branch is batch-normalized [7] or has a dropout layer (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: A new grid size reduction technique is proposed that reduces computational cost while avoiding representational bottlenecks.
key_findings.evidence: Instead of doing so, we suggest another variant the reduces the computational cost even further while removing the representational bottleneck (see Figure 10). We can use two parallel stride 2 blocks: P and C. P is a pooling layer (either average or maximum pooling) the activation, both of them are stride 2 the filter banks of which are concatenated as in figure 10 (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: Label-Smoothing Regularization (LSR) is introduced as a new regularization mechanism to encourage models to be less confident and improve generalization.
key_findings.evidence: We propose a mechanism to regularize the classifier layer by estimating the marginalized effect of label-dropout during training. We propose a mechanism for encouraging the model to be less confident. For ILSVRC 2012, we have found a consistent improvement of about 0.2% absolute both for top-1 error and the top-5 error (cf. Table 3) (Proposed Solution).

key_findings.claim: The proposed Inception-v3 architecture is computationally efficient compared to other deep networks.
key_findings.evidence: Although our network is 42 layers deep, our computation cost is only about 2.5 higher than that of GoogLeNet and it is still much more efficient than VGGNet. Our model outperforms the results of He et al [6] – cutting the top-5 (top-1) error by 25% (14%) relative, respectively – while being six times cheaper computationally and using at least five times less parameters (estimated) (Conclusion).
key_findings.limitations: Parameter count for comparison with He et al [6] is 'estimated' (Conclusion).
